To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the crystal structure of human AP endonuclease has been determined at high resolution; the structure of the human AP endonuclese has been solved at high resolution and reveals the molecular basis for its AP site specificity; and the structure of human AP site endonuclease suggests the mechanism of AP site recognition and cleavage.

HAP1 is the major AP endonuclease in human cells, that it is structurally similar to bovine DNase and to E.coli EXOIII, that it has three loop regions that are specific to itself and EXOIII, and that it recognizes AP sites by recognizing the extra‐helical sugar, and not the base opposite the AP lesion.

HAP1, the major human AP endonuclease, has a structure similar to that of bovine DNase and EXOIII, and that the structure of HAP1 suggests a mechanism for recognition of the deoxribose moiety of AP sites.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HAP1 has the potential to be an excellent target for the development of novel anticancer drugs.
the structure of HAP1 reveals the molecular basis of AP site recognition and cleavage by EXOIII and HAP1 and provides the basis for the design of novel inhibitors of these enzymes.
the HAP1 structure is the first example of a structure for a member of a family of enzymes which are involved in the repair of DNA damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the HAP1 structure provides a structural framework for understanding how this enzyme recognizes and cleaves DNA abasic sites, and that the structure provides a basis for rational design of AP endonucleases with altered specificities.
the HAP1 structure provides the first detailed view of the recognition and cleavage of AP sites in the context of the human DNA damage repair machinery.

the recognition of AP sites by HAP1 and other AP endonucleases involves the interaction of the enzyme with the deoxyribofuranose ring in an extra‐ or flipped‐in conformation, not with the AP site as a base‐pair vacancy.
